explanations.answer: Take His hand off Job and don't terrify him
explanations.explanation: Job asks God to withdraw His hand and not let His terror frighten him (Job 13:21). Those are the two. If God grants them, Job says he won't need to hide from Him (Job 13:20). He wants to stand there and talk, not duck behind the furniture.

explanations.answer: Heal Job's sores and bring back his flocks
explanations.explanation: Sores and flocks don't show up in Job's ask here. His two requests are about God's hand and God's terror: “Withdraw Your hand from me, and do not let Your terror frighten me.” (Job 13:21) That's the whole list. Think of it as a short to-do list with two lines on it.

explanations.answer: Quiet Job's friends and send Job a sign
explanations.explanation: Job has been answering his friends (Job 12:1-13:19), but right now he's turned to talk to God. His two requests are that God withdraw His hand and not let His terror frighten him (Job 13:21). No sign is on the list. Friends aren't on it either.

explanations.answer: A chance to talk it out together
explanations.explanation: Job says, “Then call me, and I will answer, or let me speak, and You can reply.” (Job 13:22) Either way, it goes back and forth. He isn't asking for a speech. I think he wants a real conversation.

explanations.answer: A promise to restore all he lost
explanations.explanation: Job doesn't ask for a promise to restore anything here. He asks that God call him and he will answer, or that he speak and God reply (Job 13:22). It's about the conversation itself. Think of it as asking for a sit-down, not a handout.

explanations.answer: A sign that his friends are mistaken
explanations.explanation: Job has been answering his friends (Job 12:1-13:19), but this verse isn't about them. He asks that God call him and he'll answer, or let him speak and God can reply (Job 13:22). The conversation he's asking for is with God. I think that tells you where Job wants his answers from.

Job asks, “Why do You hide Your face and consider me as Your enemy?” (Job 13:24) He asks it straight to God. Notice it comes out as a question, not a verdict. I think it's coming from a hurting place.

A stranger is someone you don't know, and Job doesn't use that word. The word is enemy (Job 13:24). He asks why God hides His face and considers him as one. Strangers get a polite nod, so Job's question is a lot sharper than that.

Servant is a good word, but it's not the one Job says. He asks why God considers him as His enemy (Job 13:24). That's how it feels to him, I think, which is why the question is so raw. Job is asking, not accusing out of nowhere.

Job asks, “Would You frighten a windblown leaf? Would You chase after dry chaff?” (Job 13:25) Those are two light things that the wind pushes around. I think he's showing how small he feels. Nobody sprints after a leaf.

A sheep is a living creature that can run, but Job doesn't mention one here. He says windblown leaf and dry chaff, two things the wind pushes around (Job 13:25). Chasing a sheep at least makes sense. Chasing chaff is just silly, and I think that's his point.

A fleeing deer would at least be a worthy chase. Job's picture is much smaller: a windblown leaf and dry chaff (Job 13:25). Both are light enough for the wind to push around. Nobody works up a sweat over those.

Job says God will “…bequeath to me the iniquities of my youth.” (Job 13:26) Bequeath is a fancy word for passing something down, like an inheritance. So Job feels like he's been handed a pile of old mistakes. I think that's a heavy thing to carry around.

Job does say it, so this one is true. He says God will “…bequeath to me the iniquities of my youth.” (Job 13:26) It sits right after the line about bitter accusations. The wording is fancy, so it's easy to doubt.

Job says man “…wastes away like something rotten, like a moth-eaten garment.” (Job 13:28) Picture a coat with moth holes, slowly coming apart. That's the image he gives. It's about something wearing out, not something that happens in a flash.
A stain is a different problem than moth holes. Job says man wastes away like something rotten, like a moth-eaten garment (Job 13:28). Nothing gets hidden in that picture. It's just wearing away.

Swapping it out is what you'd do with a ruined jacket, but Job doesn't say that. He says man wastes away (Job 13:28). The garment is moth-eaten, and the picture stays on the wearing away. No trip to the closet in this verse.

Job says the opposite. A man born of woman, he says, is “short of days and full of trouble.” (Job 14:1) Short days and plenty of trouble, with no long life anywhere in the sentence. I think Job says it straight from the heart.
Job sets “short of days” right beside “full of trouble.” (Job 14:1) Neither of those says long. He's describing a life as brief and hard. It's a heavy line, and it's what the text says.

Job says, “Like a flower, he comes forth, then withers away…” (Job 14:2) A flower on the counter looks great for a few days and then droops. Job sees a person's life as that quick. Up it comes, and then it fades.

A flower that returns would be nice, but that's not Job's picture. He says the flower comes forth, then withers away (Job 14:2). He's talking about how quickly a life fades. The picture only goes one way here.
A whole patch of flowers multiplying sounds lovely, but Job doesn't say that. The flower comes forth, then withers away (Job 14:2). His focus is how short a life is. No bouquet in this verse.
Job asks, “Who can bring out clean from unclean? No one!” (Job 14:4) So trying harder doesn't change it. No amount of effort shows up in that verse. You can't polish your way out of it, friend.
That's the call. Job asks who can bring out clean from unclean, then answers himself: “No one!” (Job 14:4) Effort never comes into it. The question has one answer.

explanations.answer: Look away and let him rest
explanations.explanation: Job says, “look away from him and let him rest…” (Job 14:6) This comes right after he says a man's days are determined and God has set limits he cannot exceed (Job 14:5). So he's asking for rest inside those limits. Even a hired hand gets a breather.

explanations.answer: Add more days to his life
explanations.explanation: Job doesn't ask for extra days. He says the days are determined and God has set limits he cannot exceed (Job 14:5). So his request is for rest inside those limits. It's a smaller ask than you might expect.

explanations.answer: Show him the day he will die
explanations.explanation: Job doesn't ask to see a date. He says the number of a man's months is with God (Job 14:5). His request is for God to look away and let him rest (Job 14:6). The number stays with God, and Job leaves it there.

Job says, “…If it is cut down, it will sprout again, and its tender shoots will not fail.” (Job 14:7) He calls that hope for a tree. Chop it down and it can come back. That's a tree with a real comeback story.
That's the opposite of what Job says. He says there's hope for a tree, and if it's cut down it will sprout again (Job 14:7). Its tender shoots will not fail. For a tree, the chop isn't the last word.
Hauling it off for firewood isn't in Job's picture. He says if a tree is cut down, it will sprout again (Job 14:7). He calls that hope for a tree. Job's eyes are on the stump, not the woodpile.

Job says, “…at the scent of water it will bud and put forth twigs like a sapling.” (Job 14:9) Just a whiff, and the old stump gets going. I know folks who bounce back that fast at the scent of a fresh batch of cookies. Same energy.

Sunshine is a fair guess, but Job says the scent of water (Job 14:9). The roots have grown old and the stump has died in the soil (Job 14:8). Even so, a bit of water is enough to make it bud. The sun doesn't get a mention.
Pruning is careful work, and Job's tree doesn't get any. It's the scent of water that makes it bud (Job 14:9). There's no farmer in the picture, just a stump and a whiff. The tree handles the rest.

Job says the opposite about a man: “…so a man lies down and does not rise.” (Job 14:12) The tree gets a sprout in verse 7, but Job doesn't say a man does. He adds that until the heavens are no more, he will not be awakened or roused from sleep. That's the contrast he's drawing.

False it is. Job lines up the tree and the man, then turns with “But a man dies and is laid low…” (Job 14:10) In verse 12 he says a man lies down and does not rise. He says that until the heavens are no more, the man will not be awakened. The tree and the man don't match in his picture.

explanations.answer: Set a time and remember him
explanations.explanation: Job wishes, “If only You would appoint a time for me and then remember me!” (Job 14:13) So the wish has two parts: a set time, and then being remembered. He asks it of God and no one else. I think that's a hopeful thread in a heavy stretch.

explanations.answer: Heal every one of his sores
explanations.explanation: Healing isn't what Job wishes for in this verse. Besides being hidden in Sheol until God's anger has passed, he wishes God would appoint a time for him and then remember him (Job 14:13). That's a different kind of ask. It's about timing and being remembered.

explanations.answer: Send someone else to bring him out
explanations.explanation: Job doesn't mention a rescuer here. He turns to God Himself and wishes He would appoint a time and then remember him (Job 14:13). It's God he's asking, start to finish. One name on the envelope.

Job says, “All the days of my hard service I will wait, until my renewal comes.” (Job 14:14) Wait. He doesn't say rush, and he doesn't say run. I once waited years in the back of a kitchen junk drawer, so I know waiting is no small thing.

Job has talked about hiding, and he wishes to be hidden in Sheol (Job 14:13), but fleeing isn't his plan here. He says he will wait (Job 14:14). That's all the days of his hard service, until his renewal comes. I think waiting takes real grit.

Grief runs all through this chapter, I think, but the verb here is different. Job says he will wait all the days of his hard service until his renewal comes (Job 14:14). Waiting and grieving can happen together. This verse says wait.

Job says, “You will call, and I will answer; You will desire the work of Your hands.” (Job 14:15) He speaks of God desiring the work of His hands. After the heavy lines before it, this one lifts. It's a hopeful turn.

Job does say it, so this one is true. Verse 15 reads, “You will call, and I will answer; You will desire the work of Your hands.” It follows his line about waiting for his renewal. It's a hopeful statement, and it's right there in the text.

Job says, “For then You would count my steps, but would not keep track of my sin.” (Job 14:16) Steps get counted, but sin doesn't get tracked. Earlier he said God stands watch over all his paths (Job 13:27). I think this is a very different kind of watching.

A name is a nice thing to keep track of, but Job doesn't bring one up here. He says God would count his steps but would not keep track of his sin (Job 14:16). The thing no one is keeping track of is the sin. His name never comes into it.

Prayers are a kind guess, but Job says sin (Job 14:16). He says God would count his steps and not keep track of his sin. I think Job is picturing a very different kind of record from the one he complained about earlier. That earlier record was the bitter accusations (Job 13:26).

Job says, “…You would cover over my iniquity.” (Job 14:17) His transgression is sealed in a bag, and then it's covered over. So the picture is of sin tucked away, not put on display. It's a hopeful image.

Showing it off is the reverse of Job's picture. His transgression is sealed in a bag, and God would cover over his iniquity (Job 14:17). Nothing gets held up for his friends to see. Covered means covered.

A scale is for weighing, and Job doesn't mention one. He says his transgression would be sealed in a bag and God would cover over his iniquity (Job 14:17). The sealing and covering are the actions. No measuring, just tucking away.

Job says, “…so You destroy a man’s hope.” (Job 14:19) Water wears away the stones and torrents wash away the soil, and he sets God's action beside those. This is a heavy line, friend, so I'll leave the jokes out of it. I think it comes from a painful place.

Job's comparison lands on hope, not on a name (Job 14:19). Water wears away the stones and torrents wash away the soil, so God destroys a man's hope. It's a hard thing for Job to say. I think he's speaking from a hurting place.

Pride isn't the thing in this line. Job says that as water wears away stones, so God destroys a man's hope (Job 14:19). In his picture, it's slow and steady like water on rock. Hope is what gets worn down.

Job says the opposite: “If his sons receive honor, he does not know it…” (Job 14:21) He adds that if they are brought low, the man is unaware. So good news or hard news about his sons, he doesn't know either way. It's a quiet, heavy line.

Job says, “If his sons receive honor, he does not know it; if they are brought low, he is unaware.” (Job 14:21) So honor or hardship for his sons, the man is unaware of both. This is Job describing it, and I think it comes from a sad place. It's a heavy verse.

Job says, “He feels only the pain of his own body and mourns only for himself.” (Job 14:22) So the pain he names is in the body. It's the last verse of this stretch, and I think it ends on a lonely note. Job is wrapping up a heavy thought.

The verse before talks about sons (Job 14:21), so family is a fair guess. But Job ends with the pain of his own body (Job 14:22). He says a man mourns only for himself. The sons were in the verse before, and he says the man doesn't know about them.

Job's friends have been all over this conversation (Job 12:1-13:19), but they aren't in this verse. He says a man feels only the pain of his own body and mourns only for himself (Job 14:22). It's a lonely ending. Friends aren't part of that final picture.
